draft.title: Matrices as transformations
card: A 2 × 2 matrix can move every point (x, y) in the plane. Write the point as a column and multiply: [a b; c d] times (x, y) gives (ax + by, cx + dy).
The first column of the matrix is where the point (1, 0) lands. The second column is where (0, 1) lands.

Some common matrices: [k 0; 0 k] is a dilation by factor k from the origin. [1 0; 0 −1] reflects in the x-axis. [0 −1; 1 0] rotates 90° anticlockwise about the origin. [1 k; 0 1] is a shear that moves points parallel to the x-axis.
Example: [2 0; 0 2] sends (3, 1) to (2×3 + 0×1, 0×3 + 2×1) = (6, 2). Every coordinate doubles.
draft.remember: Multiply the matrix by the point's column. The columns show where (1, 0) and (0, 1) go.

a.q: What does the matrix [1 0; 0 −1] do to the point (4, 3)?
a.why: The new point is (1×4 + 0×3, 0×4 + (−1)×3) = (4, −3). The x-value stays and the y-value changes sign, so this is a reflection in the x-axis. Reflection in the y-axis would give (−4, 3).
a.clue: Multiply each row of the matrix by the column (4, 3).

b.q: A matrix sends (1, 0) to (0, 1) and (0, 1) to (−1, 0). Where does it send the point (2, 5)?
b.why: The columns are (0, 1) and (−1, 0), so the matrix is [0 −1; 1 0], a 90° anticlockwise rotation. Then (2, 5) goes to (0×2 + (−1)×5, 1×2 + 0×5) = (−5, 2). Putting the columns in as rows would give (5, −2).
b.clue: Where (1, 0) and (0, 1) land are the columns of the matrix.
